subject: Post-call: Tool/Function Calling Integration Patterns & Next Steps
messages:
From: Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@finapps.com>
To: marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: Fri, 6 Mar 2026 16:10:00 -0700
Subject: Follow-up + architecture questions re: tool calling patterns

Thanks for running the call today — helpful conversation. A quick follow-up with a summary from our side and a few architecture questions before we run the engineering spike: 

Summary (from our notes):
- Goal: surface finance data and run candidate lookups + structured actions (create transaction, fetch invoice) from a single conversational UX.
- Interested in: tool/function calling for deterministic actions, embeddings + reranker for doc retrieval, and parallel tool patterns for eligibility checks.

Questions we want to validate in the spike:
1) Tool definitions: should we define tools as lightweight HTTP endpoints or packaged lambdas? recommendations?
2) Auth: what's the recommended approach for service-to-service calls from Redwood SDK to our backend (client secrets? short-lived JWT?).
3) Parallel tools: can we call multiple tools in parallel (e.g., eligibility check, risk check) and aggregate results before rendering to user?
4) Error handling: how do we best model partial failures (one tool times out) in the assistant's structured output?
5) Embeddings/reranker: preferred pattern for candidate generation vs. reranking for precision in finance data retrieval?

We can run a 2-3 day spike if we get clear guidance on patterns and a short sample flow. Would you send a recommended integration checklist and example tool definition?

Thanks,
Alex
Director, Integrations — FinApps

--
Alex Rivera
FinApps

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@finapps.com>
Cc: Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.ai>, Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 6 Mar 2026 17:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Follow-up + architecture questions re: tool calling patterns

Thanks Alex — great questions. Below is a concise post-call recap and a recommended integration pattern you can use for the spike. I've attached a short integration guide and a sample YAML with tool definitions.

Post-call recap (high level):
- Primary flow: User query -> embeddings-only candidate retrieval -> lightweight reranker -> orchestration layer issues tool/function calls (some parallel) -> structured output returned to client.
- Non-negotiable: every tool must return a typed, JSON-serializable response (schema-backed) so the assistant can safely compose follow-up steps.

Recommended integration checklist (spike-friendly):
1) SDK setup
   - Use Redwood SDK (node/python). Example: pip install redwood-sdk or npm i @redwoodai/sdk
   - Init with service account key or API key: redwood.init({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, project: 'finapps-spike' })

2) Auth patterns
   - Short-lived service JWTs: we recommend the following for server-to-server calls: Redwood issues an exchange token scoped to "tool:invoke" that your backend validates. This avoids long-lived secrets in your tool endpoints.
   - Alternatively, you can keep tool endpoints behind your own auth and configure Redwood to attach a signed proxy token when invoking. We'll supply sample code in the guide.

3) Tool definitions + choice
   - Model tool definitions as a small contract: name, input_schema, output_schema, timeout_ms, retry_policy, idempotent flag. See attached sample_tool_definitions.yaml.
   - Prefer HTTP endpoints for quick spikes (lightweight containers or serverless). For high-throughput, consider colocated lambdas/GRPC endpoints to reduce latency.
   - Rudimentary example: 
     - create_transaction(input) -> { transaction_id, status }
     - fetch_invoice(invoice_id) -> { invoice, pdf_url }

4) Routing and parallel execution
   - Redwood's orchestration can dispatch multiple independent tool calls in parallel and aggregate results. Pattern: orchestration layer spawns parallel tasks, waits for a quorum or all, and then synthesizes a single structured output.
   - For eligibility/risk checks: run in parallel and return a merged decision object (e.g., {eligibility: true, risk_score: 0.12, details: [...] }).

5) Structured output & tool calling in the assistant
   - Use a schema-first approach: assistant returns a typed object with either "invoke_tool" actions or final_text. Example: { action: "invoke_tool", tool: "fetch_invoice", args: { invoice_id: "123" } }
   - When multiple actions are possible, prefer returning a prioritized list. Redwood can execute the top-N automatically or surface options to the user.

6) Error handling & partial failures
   - Tool responses must include status and optional error_code. Pattern for partial failure: include a "partial_results" array + "failed_tools" with error metadata. Example: { results: [...], failed_tools: [{name: 'risk_check', code: 'timeout', message: 'took >500ms'}] }
   - Retries: keep retry policy conservative for non-idempotent tools. We recommend: idempotent=true -> retry 2x with exponential backoff; idempotent=false -> no automatic retry, surface to user or queue for manual retry.

7) Embeddings + reranker
   - Candidate generation: use approximate nearest neighbor (FAISS/pinecone) with lightweight embedding model to return top-K candidates (K=50 for initial).
   - Reranker: call a fine-tuned or instruction-tuned model to rescore top-K (K=10) preserving latency SLOs. Rerankers should operate on the candidate set and return a score and a justification field if possible.
   - If you need strict precision (finance workflows), add a secondary verification tool that runs deterministic checks against canonical data.

8) Observability & instrumentation
   - Attach tool call metadata to Redwood traces (latency, success, token usage). We'll provide a sample tracing hook in the guide.

Next steps we propose for the spike (2-3 work days):
- Day 0: Shared repo + API creds (we'll provide a scoped test API key).
- Day 1: Implement 2 example tools as HTTP endpoints (fetch_invoice, eligibility_check) and wire up SDK calls.
- Day 2: Add embeddings candidate flow + simple reranker; run end-to-end test with sample prompts and inspect structured output.

I've attached: redwood-integration-guide.pdf (quickstart + sample hooks) and sample_tool_definitions.yaml.

If that sounds good, we'll send a scoped test API key and a short repo template.

Cheers,
Marissa Cole
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

From: Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.ai>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@finapps.com>
Date: Fri, 6 Mar 2026 18:15:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Follow-up + architecture questions re: tool calling patterns

Couple of quick technical clarifications from our infra/SDK side that we'll want to lock for the spike:

- Rate limits & backpressure: we'll expose per-tool concurrency limits at the Redwood routing layer. Alex, do you have expected QPS per tool for the spike? We can default to 10 rps and tune.
- Webhook / async tools: support for fire-and-forget tools is available, but we recommend using a callback URL pattern: Redwood will POST a result to a supplied callback when the tool completes. This is useful for long-running background checks.
- Function signatures: prefer JSON Schema draft-07 for input/output. It makes runtime validation simple and keeps the assistant from producing malformed tool args.
- Timeout guidance: for a 300ms SLO on user-visible actions, aim for tool timeouts <=250ms at the endpoint and let orchestration aggregate. For long-running checks, use async + callback.

Alex: if you can share a rough QPS/latency target for each of the candidate tools, we will pre-configure the routing policies and sample env vars in the repo template.

Thanks,
Dev
